strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: improving precision and robustness of autoregressive vision-language-action policies at test time without training a separate verifier.

The method is simple and practical: sample multiple action candidates and rank them using an internal condition-masking KL confidence signal, with an efficient single-prefill deployment variant to reduce latency.
The paper evaluates across several relevant robotics benchmarks and settings, including RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, and small-scale real-robot experiments.
Ablations study candidate count, masking variants, joint training, reference temperature, aggregation strategy, and latency, giving useful empirical insight into when the method works.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The work is largely an adaptation of Best-of-N/self-certainty style test-time selection to autoregressive VLAs, with condition masking as the reference distribution. The conceptual advance over existing verifier-free confidence or entropy/KL ranking methods is not deeply established.

The evaluation protocol appears heavily tuned: the paper searches over sampling temperature, number of candidates, masking variant, and reference temperature, then reports the best result for each policy/dataset. It is unclear whether these choices are selected on validation tasks, test tasks, or by test-set performance, which weakens the evidence.

Main gains are often modest or inconsistent outside selected low-data/high-precision cases: SIMPLER improves from 46.9 to 50.3 average, LIBERO from 92.0 to 93.1 for pi0-FAST, and OpenVLA degrades on Spatial and Goal while slightly improving average. Some task categories in RoboCasa also show minimal or negative changes.

The comparison to the most relevant alternative class, external verifier/value-guided test-time scaling for robotics, is mostly qualitative. There is no direct empirical comparison under matched compute, demonstrations, or latency, making it hard to assess the practical advantage.

MG-Select and MG-Select* are somewhat confounded: the strongest results often include joint training, which is no longer purely test-time and may itself act as regularization. The paper does not always isolate whether improvements come from sampling/ranking, condition-dropout training, or hyperparameter tuning.

The real-world experiments are encouraging but small: only a few tasks, 16 or 24 trials per reported condition, no confidence intervals or statistical tests, and limited description of randomization, failure modes, or robustness across scenes.

The method has several brittle design choices, including which conditions to mask, the KL direction, high reference temperature, and first-token aggregation. These are empirically selected and not strongly justified theoretically, raising concerns about transfer to other VLA architectures or tokenizers.

Reproducibility is incomplete for a top-tier submission: implementation details are provided, but there is no mention of code/model release, validation protocol, exact hardware latency setup beyond a single benchmark, or enough detail to independently reproduce the real-world setup.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: improving precision and robustness of autoregressive vision-language-action models at test time without training a separate verifier.

The proposed MG-Select idea is simple and practically appealing: sample multiple candidate action sequences and rank them using an internal confidence signal derived from condition-masked model distributions.

The paper evaluates on several robotics benchmarks, including RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, and small-scale real-world Franka experiments, which is a broader empirical setting than many robotics papers provide.

The authors include useful ablations over inference strategy, number of candidates, masking variant, joint training, reference-distribution temperature, aggregation strategy, and latency optimization.
The single-prefill deployment optimization is a practically relevant addition, since naive best-of-N sampling can be too slow for real robot control.
weaknesses: The main technical novelty is limited. MG-Select largely combines best-of-N sampling, self-confidence/KL-style scoring, input masking, and dropout-style joint training; the paper does not provide a strong conceptual or theoretical argument for why KL from a condition-masked distribution should reliably identify better robot actions.

The central framing is somewhat inconsistent. The paper emphasizes verifier-free test-time scaling without additional training, but its strongest results often rely on MG-Select*, which uses an additional joint training strategy with condition dropout. This weakens the claimed simplicity and makes the pure test-time contribution less compelling.

The evaluation protocol raises fairness concerns. Appendix A says hyperparameters are searched over multiple temperatures, candidate counts, masking variants, and regularization temperatures, and the best result is reported for each policy, but the paper does not clearly describe validation splits, selection criteria, or whether baselines receive comparable tuning budgets.

The empirical gains are mixed and often modest. On LIBERO, the average improvements are small, and some individual suites degrade; on SIMPLER-WidowX the improvement is only a few percentage points on a 24-trial evaluation; on RoboCasa gains are larger mainly in low-data settings and with joint training.

The paper lacks strong comparisons to the most relevant verifier-based test-time scaling robotics methods under the same models and tasks. Citing external results from other papers is not sufficient to establish that MG-Select is competitive with trained verifiers or other action-selection strategies under controlled conditions.

The real-world evaluation is too small to support broad claims about robustness or out-of-distribution generalization. The OOD setting has only two tasks and 16 trials per task, with no statistical tests or confidence intervals despite noisy robot execution.

Ablations suggest fragility rather than robustness. Performance depends on non-obvious choices such as using only the first 5 tokens, applying a high regularization temperature to the masked distribution, and choosing task-specific masking variants. These choices are not well justified and may limit transfer to other VLA tokenizers or tasks.

The method’s confidence score is under-explained technically. Selecting actions with high KL(Q||P) from a masked reference can reward distributions that differ from the reference, but the connection between this divergence and actual action correctness is only intuitive and not validated with calibration or correlation analysis.

Claims of broad generality are stronger than the evidence. Most experiments are pick-and-place or precision-oriented manipulation tasks, so it remains unclear whether the method helps long-horizon reasoning, contact-rich manipulation, multi-stage language-conditioned tasks, or settings where diversity rather than confidence is needed.

Reproducibility is incomplete. While some training details are provided, key implementation details for scoring, masking at inference, candidate decoding, validation selection, and statistical variability are insufficient for confident reproduction from the manuscript alone.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and practical verifier-free test-time scaling method for autoregressive VLA policies, using KL divergence from masked-condition reference distributions to rank sampled action candidates. The idea is simple, well-motivated, and directly targets an important bottleneck in high-precision robot manipulation.

The empirical coverage is a major strength: experiments span RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, two VLA backbones, and real-world Franka experiments. The consistent direction of improvement across simulation and real-world settings makes the contribution credible.

The ablation section is useful and fairly complete, covering candidate count, inference strategy, masking variants, joint training, regularization temperature, aggregation strategy, and latency. This helps isolate why the method works and what design choices matter.

The real-world results, though limited in scale, are valuable. Gains on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution pick-and-place tasks support the claim that the method can improve precision beyond simulation.
The method is deployment-conscious: the single-prefill variant addresses the obvious latency concern for best-of-N sampling and shows that the additional inference cost can be controlled.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than transformative. The core method is a robotics adaptation of best-of-N/self-certainty style selection, and the paper would benefit from a sharper conceptual distinction from prior verifier-free confidence or uncertainty-ranking methods.

The strongest results often rely on the proposed joint training strategy, which weakens the framing that the method requires no additional training. MG-Select without joint training is evaluated in some settings, but the headline improvements frequently use MG-Select*, making the practical contribution somewhat less purely test-time than advertised.

The evaluation lacks direct comparison to the most relevant external-verifier test-time scaling methods under matched settings. Since the paper positions itself against verifier-based approaches, a same-backbone or same-benchmark comparison would substantially strengthen the evidence.

Some improvements are modest in absolute terms, especially on SIMPLER-WidowX and LIBERO. For example, average LIBERO gains are small, and OpenVLA has mixed suite-level results. The paper should be more measured about generality and significance.

Hyperparameter selection appears to report the best configuration per dataset after searching over temperatures, candidate counts, masking variants, and regularization temperatures. Without a clearly separated validation protocol, this raises concern about benchmark-specific tuning and optimistic reported gains.

The real-world evaluation uses relatively few tasks and trials, with no statistical uncertainty reported. The results are promising but not yet strong enough to fully establish robust real-world generalization.

The method is specialized to autoregressive action-token VLAs and depends on tokenizer-specific aggregation choices, such as using the first 5 tokens for π0-FAST. This limits immediate generality and suggests some fragility across action representations.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: improving VLA action precision at test time without training an external verifier.
The proposed MG-Select method is simple, broadly applicable to autoregressive VLAs, and practically motivated by internal distributional confidence under condition masking.
Evaluation is reasonably broad, covering RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, CALVIN, and real-world Franka experiments, with multiple VLA backbones in simulation.
Ablations study several relevant factors, including number of candidates, masking variant, joint training, reference temperature, aggregation strategy, and deployment latency.
The single-prefill deployment discussion is useful and makes the test-time scaling approach more practical.
weaknesses: The central scoring rule is heuristic: the paper does not convincingly justify why larger KL from a masked-condition distribution should reliably correspond to better actions, beyond empirical observations.
Reported gains are often modest or inconsistent outside the lowest-data RoboCasa setting, e.g. small average gains on SIMPLER-WidowX and LIBERO, with some task-suite regressions.

Hyperparameters and masking variants are searched per dataset and the best result is reported, but the paper does not clearly separate validation from test evaluation, raising concerns about benchmark-level overfitting.

Comparisons to prior methods are not fully satisfying: many baselines are taken from papers with different training setups, and the RoboMonkey comparison modifies that method, limiting conclusions about relative performance.
Real-world experiments are encouraging but small-scale, with limited trials and task diversity, so the claimed robustness and OOD generalization remain only partially supported.

The joint-training variant requires additional fine-tuning with condition dropout, which weakens the framing of the approach as purely test-time and makes it harder to isolate the contribution of the selection metric.

Reproducibility is incomplete: implementation details are given, but there is no clear statement about code release, validation protocol, random seed variability beyond averages, or statistical significance/confidence intervals.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: improving precision and robustness of autoregressive vision-language-action policies at test time without training an external verifier.
The proposed method is simple and practical: sample multiple action candidates and rank them using a condition-masked reference distribution, with a latency-aware single-prefill deployment variant.
The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, CALVIN, and a small real-world Franka setup.
The paper includes useful ablations over number of candidates, masking variants, joint training, temperature, aggregation strategy, dropout ratio, and model scale.
weaknesses: The main claims are overstated relative to the evidence. Many gains are small in absolute terms, especially on SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, CALVIN, and 300-demo RoboCasa, while the paper emphasizes large relative improvements from low baselines.

A major confound is joint training: on RoboCasa, joint imitation learning alone improves pick-and-place from 17.0 to 28.5, while MG-Select* reaches 31.0. The paper’s headline comparisons often attribute gains to MG-Select even though much of the improvement comes from an altered training procedure.

The method appears heavily tuned per benchmark. Appendix A states that sampling temperature, candidate count, masking variant, and regularization temperature are searched and the best result is reported for each policy; this raises concern about test-set selection and weakens claims of generality.

Baselines are not consistently controlled. Several comparisons use numbers taken from prior papers, and the RoboMonkey comparison modifies that method by removing Gaussian perturbation and majority voting, making the comparison hard to interpret.

The real-world evaluation is too small to support strong robustness/generalization claims: 24 trials per ID task and 16 trials per OOD task, with no confidence intervals, statistical tests, or detailed failure analysis.

The core technical contribution is incremental: it adapts Best-of-N/self-certainty ideas to VLAs using masked-condition KL, but the justification for why KL(Q||P) should identify better actions remains mostly heuristic.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty reporting despite high-variance robotic benchmarks. Results averaged over seeds are reported, but no standard deviations or confidence intervals are provided for most tables.
The method can hurt performance in some settings, such as LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal, and the paper does not provide a principled criterion for when MG-Select should be applied versus avoided.

Reproducibility is incomplete: implementation details are given, but there is no clear commitment to releasing code, checkpoints, data collection details for real-world tasks, or exact validation protocol for hyperparameter selection.

strengths: Timely and practically relevant problem: improving autoregressive VLA action precision at test time without relying on a separately trained verifier is important for robotics deployment.
The proposed KL-based selection against masked-condition reference distributions is simple, intuitive, and broadly applicable to autoregressive VLAs.
Evaluation is unusually broad: RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, CALVIN, and real-world Franka experiments, with multiple base models including pi0-FAST, OpenVLA, and MiniVLA.
Ablations are reasonably comprehensive, covering candidate count, masking variants, joint training, reference-temperature regularization, aggregation strategy, dropout ratio, and latency.
The paper is clearly written, and the method is easy to understand and likely implementable from the provided details.
The real-world results, though limited, support the main claim that the approach can improve precision beyond simulation.
weaknesses: The main empirical gains are often modest outside low-data RoboCasa: e.g., SIMPLER improves from 46.9 to 50.3, pi0-FAST on LIBERO from 92.0 to 93.1, and CALVIN average length from 3.69 to 3.86. This makes the impact somewhat incremental despite the broad evaluation.

The paper repeatedly emphasizes verifier-free test-time scaling without additional training, but the strongest results generally use MG-Select* with joint training. The distinction between purely test-time improvement and training-assisted improvement should be clearer and more central in the claims.

Hyperparameters are searched per dataset/policy and the best result is reported, including masking type, temperature, candidate count, and aggregation. Without a validation protocol or held-out tuning split, there is a risk of benchmark overfitting.
The real-world evaluation has small trial counts and lacks confidence intervals or significance testing, so the robustness of the reported 28% and 35% relative gains is uncertain.

Comparison to external-verifier methods is limited. The RoboMonkey comparison is modified by removing parts of that method, and most main tables compare against reported baselines rather than strong reproduced test-time-scaling baselines under matched compute.

The proposed confidence metric is heuristic. The entropy-temperature derivation is correct but does not really justify why maximizing KL from a masked distribution should correlate with action success; more diagnostic evidence would strengthen the technical argument.

Some results show regressions on individual suites/tasks, such as LIBERO-Spatial/Goal and parts of SIMPLER, suggesting the method can add harmful stochasticity when the base policy is already strong. The paper acknowledges this but does not provide a robust selection or fallback mechanism.
